checks.label: App credentials expired or expiring within 30 days
checks.fix: On each affected app, create the replacement secret or certificate before expiry, update every consumer, then delete the old credential. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Certificates & secrets. SAML signing certs: Enterprise apps > (app) > Single sign-on.
checks.impact: A secret or certificate that lapses takes the sign-in or integration down with it. An expired SAML signing certificate locks every user out of that application until it is replaced. Credentials left behind after they expire hide the ones that still matter.
checks.best_practice: Renew at least 30 days before expiry, so there is room for a change window. SAML signing certificates want more: stage the replacement and notify the relying party well ahead, because activating one breaks sign-in for everyone if it is rushed. Delete credentials that have already expired: they authenticate nothing, so removing them needs no change window and only leaves a cleaner credential list behind.
checks.blurb: Secrets and certificates on app registrations and enterprise applications (SAML token-signing certificates included) that lapse in the next 30 days, plus any that have already lapsed.

checks.label: Long-lived app credentials (> 2 years)
checks.fix: On each app, replace the long-lived credential with a new secret or certificate expiring within 24 months (12 preferred), or add a federated credential and delete the secret entirely. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Certificates & secrets.
checks.impact: App passwords and certificates that stay valid for years give anyone who steals one a long, quiet window into your environment.
checks.best_practice: Two years is the maximum; 6 to 12 months where rotation won't create friction. Better still, drop the secret entirely and use a federated (workload identity) credential, which has nothing to leak and nothing to rotate.
checks.blurb: App secrets/certs with a lifetime over 730 days that are still active.

checks.label: Multi-tenant app registrations
checks.fix: Set the app's signInAudience to AzureADMyOrg unless multi-tenant access is genuinely required and reviewed. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Manifest (signInAudience property). CLI: Update-MgApplication -ApplicationId <objId> -SignInAudience AzureADMyOrg.
checks.impact: Apps open to outside accounts can be signed into from organizations you don't control, widening who can reach your data.
checks.best_practice: Single-tenant unless the app is deliberately sold or shared outside the organisation. If it must be multi-tenant, pair it with a publisher verification and restrict who can consent.
checks.blurb: Apps whose sign-in audience allows accounts outside this tenant.

checks.label: Apps with multiple secrets
checks.fix: On each app, keep one active client secret and delete the surplus ones once no consumer still uses them. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Certificates & secrets > Client secrets. CLI: Remove-MgApplicationPassword -ApplicationId <objId> -KeyId <keyId>.
checks.impact: Extra credentials on an app mean more copies to leak and no way to tell who is using which one.
checks.best_practice: One active secret per app. A second is expected only briefly, during a rollover; remove the old one as soon as every consumer has moved.
checks.blurb: App registrations holding more than one client secret.

checks.label: SPA apps holding client secrets
checks.fix: On each SPA app, delete every client secret; a single-page app authenticates with the authorization-code + PKCE flow and must carry no secret. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Certificates & secrets > Client secrets > Delete.
checks.impact: A browser app cannot keep a secret; anyone who inspects it can extract the credential and act as the app.
checks.best_practice: A single-page app runs entirely in the browser, so it has nowhere to hide a secret; it should authenticate with the authorization-code flow plus PKCE and carry no client secret or certificate at all.
checks.blurb: Single-page apps (public clients) that carry active secrets, which they must not.

checks.label: Azure DevOps (azdo*) apps with active secrets
checks.fix: Convert each azdo* Azure Resource Manager service connection to workload identity federation, then delete the app registration's client secret. Portal: Azure DevOps > Project settings > Service connections > (connection) > Convert.
checks.impact: Pipeline credentials that never rotate end up in logs and repositories; federation removes the stored secret entirely.
checks.best_practice: Pipeline identities should authenticate with workload identity federation rather than a stored secret, which has nothing to leak and never has to be rotated; where a secret is genuinely unavoidable, keep its lifetime short and rotate it on a schedule.
checks.blurb: azdo* service-connection apps still using secrets instead of federation.

checks.label: DevOps-managed apps off the azdo* naming convention
checks.fix: Rename each DevOps-managed app to the azdo* convention, or correct its internal notes so governance tooling can find it. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Branding & properties > Name. CLI: Update-MgApplication -ApplicationId <objId> -DisplayName 'azdo-<name>'.
checks.impact: Unlabelled automation apps are easy to mistake for user apps, so they escape reviews and cleanup.
checks.best_practice: Pick one naming convention, write it down, and let automation depend on it. Here the convention is that anything Azure DevOps manages is prefixed 'azdo'; the prefix is what lets an operator tell at a glance which app registrations are safe to touch by hand and which belong to a pipeline.
checks.blurb: Apps marked Azure DevOps-managed in notes but not named azdo*.

checks.label: Guests with password-only authentication
checks.fix: Create a Conditional Access policy including All guest and external users with Grant access, Require multifactor authentication, so each guest must register a second factor at next sign-in. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: External guests protected by only a password are the easiest door into your tenant for phishing and password-spray attacks.
checks.best_practice: Every guest should have a strong second factor, not a password alone; require MFA for guests through Conditional Access so an external account cannot be taken over with a single stolen or sprayed password.
checks.blurb: Guest users whose only registered method is a password (no MFA).

checks.label: Privileged account sign-in & auth audit
checks.fix: Create a Conditional Access policy targeting Directory roles with Grant access, Require authentication strength, Phishing-resistant MFA strength; remove stale admin assignments and move standing access to PIM eligibility. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies.
checks.impact: One phished administrator without strong sign-in protection can hand over the entire tenant.
checks.best_practice: Administrators should sign in with phishing-resistant MFA (an authenticator or FIDO2 key, not SMS) and hold their rights through PIM rather than permanently; an admin dormant beyond 90 days, or protected by a password alone, should have that access removed or hardened.
checks.blurb: Members of privileged directory roles, their MFA strength and last sign-in.

checks.label: PIM role activation policy
checks.fix: Require MFA (and approval for sensitive roles) on activation and set Activation maximum duration to 8 hours or less in each privileged role's PIM settings. Portal: Entra admin center > ID Governance > Privileged Identity Management > Microsoft Entra roles > Roles > select role > Role settings > Edit.
checks.impact: Admin rights that activate too easily or stay active too long defeat the point of just-in-time access.
checks.best_practice: Activating a privileged role should demand MFA and, for the most sensitive roles, approval, and the activation window should be short: cap it at 8 hours, ideally 4, so rights expire soon after the task is done rather than sitting active all day.
checks.blurb: PIM activation settings: duration too long, or no MFA/approval on activation.

checks.label: Service principals with over-privileged Graph permissions
checks.fix: On each service principal, revoke write-scoped Graph application permissions (Directory.ReadWrite.All etc.) and grant least-privilege read scopes instead. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > (app) > Permissions > Admin consent > ... > Revoke permission.
checks.impact: These automation identities could read or rewrite your entire directory; one compromised app becomes a full tenant breach.
checks.best_practice: Application permissions should be the least the workload needs and read-only wherever possible; write-scoped directory permissions such as Directory.ReadWrite.All effectively make the app an administrator, so grant a narrower scope or use delegated access instead.
checks.blurb: SPs granted high-risk application Graph roles (Directory.ReadWrite.All, etc.).

checks.label: Risky tenant-wide OAuth2 consent grants
checks.fix: Revoke the tenant-wide (AllPrincipals) delegated grant for each sensitive scope and re-grant per app or per user after review. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > (app) > Permissions > Admin consent > ... > Revoke permission.
checks.impact: A consent granted for everyone lets one app read sensitive data on behalf of every user, silently and tenant-wide.
checks.best_practice: Sensitive mailbox, file and directory scopes should not be consented tenant-wide for every user; grant them per-app after review, prefer incremental or per-user consent, and keep the scope to the minimum the app genuinely reads.
checks.blurb: Admin-consented (AllPrincipals) delegated grants for sensitive Graph scopes.

checks.label: Dormant service principals (90+ days)
checks.fix: Disable each unused service principal (set Enabled for users to sign-in to No) after confirming no automation depends on it; delete once safe. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > (app) > Properties. CLI: Update-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId <id> -AccountEnabled:$false.
checks.impact: Automation accounts nobody uses anymore are unwatched credentials an attacker can take over without anyone noticing.
checks.best_practice: A service principal with no sign-in for 90 days should be treated as unused: confirm nothing depends on it, then disable it and delete it once you are sure, so an idle credential cannot be quietly taken over.
checks.blurb: Enabled, tenant-owned SPs with no successful sign-in in 90 days (beta signInActivity).

checks.label: Apps without a verified publisher
checks.fix: Complete publisher verification by adding your Partner One ID to each externally offered app, or restrict internal apps to single-tenant. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > (app) > Branding & properties > Add Partner ID to verify publisher.
checks.impact: Apps from unverified publishers give you no assurance about who actually operates the software touching your data.
checks.best_practice: Any app offered beyond your own tenant should carry a verified publisher, which ties the software to a Microsoft-checked identity; if the app is only used internally, restrict it to single-tenant so the requirement no longer applies.
checks.blurb: Multi-tenant/published apps with no verified publisher set.

checks.label: Service principals without owners
checks.fix: Assign at least one (ideally two) accountable owners to each service principal so someone is responsible for its credentials and access. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > (app) > Owners > Add. CLI: New-MgServicePrincipalOwnerByRef -ServicePrincipalId <id>.
checks.impact: When nobody owns an identity, nobody rotates its credentials, reviews its access, or notices when it misbehaves.
checks.best_practice: Every service principal should have at least one named owner, and ideally two, so someone is always accountable for rotating its credentials, reviewing its access and noticing when it misbehaves.
checks.blurb: Tenant-owned service principals with no assigned owner.

checks.label: OAuth2 grants to third-party apps
checks.fix: Review each third-party app's consented scopes; revoke unused or over-broad grants and prefer per-user consent over tenant-wide. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > (app) > Permissions > Admin consent > ... > Revoke permission.
checks.impact: Outside vendors holding access to your users' data are part of your attack surface; each grant deserves a periodic review.
checks.best_practice: Access granted to non-Microsoft APIs is part of your attack surface and should be reviewed on a regular cadence; revoke grants no longer in use and prefer per-user consent over a tenant-wide grant.
checks.blurb: Consent grants to non-Microsoft resource apps for sensitive scopes.

checks.label: Inactive users (90+ days)
checks.fix: After manager confirmation, disable each stale account by clearing Account enabled, then delete after a grace period. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Users > All users > select user > Account status > Edit. CLI: Update-MgUser -UserId <id> -AccountEnabled:$false.
checks.impact: Dormant accounts still hold licences and access; they cost money every month and are prime targets for takeover.
checks.best_practice: An enabled account with no successful sign-in for 90 days should be reviewed and, once the manager confirms, disabled and later removed, freeing its licence and closing an easy takeover target.
checks.blurb: Enabled member accounts with no successful sign-in in 90 days.

checks.label: Inactive guest users (120+ days)
checks.fix: Remove each stale guest, then create a recurring guest access review scoped to Inactive users only (120 days) with auto-apply set to remove access. Portal: Entra admin center > Identity Governance > Access Reviews > New access review. CLI: Remove-MgUser -UserId <id>.
checks.impact: Guests who left the project long ago still hold a key to your data, and nobody is watching their accounts.
checks.best_practice: A guest who has not signed in for 120 days has almost certainly finished the work they were invited for; remove them, and run periodic guest access reviews so external accounts do not accumulate unnoticed.
checks.blurb: Accepted guest accounts with no sign-in in 120 days.

checks.label: Overdue / expiring access reviews
checks.min_role: Global Reader (+ Security Reader for role-scoped reviews)
checks.fix: Open each overdue review, collect the outstanding decisions, then Stop and Apply so the results take effect; keep recurring reviews running for privileged roles and guests. Portal: Entra admin center > ID Governance > Access Reviews > select review.
checks.impact: When access reviews lapse, leavers and role-changers keep permissions they should have lost.
checks.best_practice: Access reviews should be completed by their due date rather than left to lapse; keep recurring reviews running for privileged roles and guests so people who change teams or leave lose access promptly.
checks.blurb: Access review definitions past or near their end date with work outstanding. Reviews scoped to Entra roles are only visible with Security Reader or higher.

checks.label: Ownerless Microsoft 365 groups
checks.fix: Assign at least two owners to each group and enable the ownerless group policy (check 'When there's no owner, email and ask active group members to become an owner'). Portal: Microsoft 365 admin center > Settings > Org settings > Services > Microsoft 365 Groups.
checks.impact: Groups with no owner keep granting access with nobody accountable for who is in them.
checks.best_practice: Every Microsoft 365 group should have at least two owners; enable the ownerless-group policy so members are prompted to take ownership, rather than leaving the group granting access with nobody accountable for who is in it.
checks.blurb: Microsoft 365 groups with no owner assigned.

checks.label: Ownerless app registrations
checks.fix: On each app registration, add at least two owners you would trust with the app's permissions (Owners > Add owners). Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > App registrations > select app > Owners > Add owners.
checks.impact: An app nobody owns keeps its access forever; there is no one to ask whether it is still needed.
checks.best_practice: Aim for at least two owners per app registration (Microsoft's own guidance), so credential and lifecycle accountability survive one owner leaving. Owner is itself a privileged role, not a passive label: an owner can add credentials to the app and, since the app may hold more Graph or API permissions than the owner does personally, use them to inherit that access. The mitigation is restricting who can become an owner to people you'd trust with the app's actual permissions, not leaving the app ownerless. An ownerless app still keeps its access indefinitely, just with nobody accountable for it.
checks.blurb: App registrations with no assigned owner.

checks.label: Service principals in high-risk directory roles
checks.fix: Remove the admin role from each service principal (check it in the role's assignment list, Remove assignment) and grant least-privilege Graph permissions instead. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Roles & admins > select role. CLI: Remove-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleAssignment -UnifiedRoleAssignmentId <id>.
checks.impact: An automation identity holding an admin role is a standing target: steal its credential and you are the administrator.
checks.best_practice: Workload identities should not hold Global Administrator or similar directory roles; grant the specific least-privilege permissions the automation needs, because a standing admin role on a service principal is a credential worth stealing.
checks.blurb: Workload identities holding Global Admin / Security Admin / etc.

checks.label: Service principals with multiple sensitive app roles
checks.fix: On each service principal, revoke the excess application permissions and split workloads so each principal keeps one task's grants. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > select app > Permissions > Admin consent > Revoke permission. CLI: Remove-MgServicePrincipalAppRoleAssignedTo -ServicePrincipalId <id> -AppRoleAssignmentId <id>.
checks.impact: Identities that stack several powerful permissions concentrate risk; one leak exposes everything they can touch.
checks.best_practice: A single workload identity should not accumulate several high-privilege Graph permissions; split the work so each principal holds only what its own task requires, limiting what one leaked credential can reach.
checks.blurb: SPs assigned more than one high-privilege application role.

checks.label: Unclassified managed identities
checks.fix: Tag each managed identity (or its parent resource) with owner and workload tags via Add tags, then Save. Portal: Azure portal > select resource > Tags. CLI: az tag update --resource-id <id> --operation Merge --tags owner=<team> workload=<app>.
checks.impact: Untraceable identities slow down incident response because nobody knows what they are for or who to call.
checks.best_practice: Every managed identity carries an owner and its workload in tags or notes, recorded when it is created. Identities are cheap to make and impossible to attribute later, so an untagged one eventually becomes something nobody dares delete and nobody can justify keeping.
checks.blurb: Managed-identity SPs with no tags/notes for ownership traceability.

checks.label: Users can register applications
checks.fix: Set Users can register applications to No, then grant the Application Developer role to the named users who still need to register apps. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Users > User settings.
checks.impact: When any user can register apps, consent-phishing and shadow applications multiply with nobody reviewing them.
checks.best_practice: App registration should be limited to administrators or a delegated group rather than open to every user, so new applications and the consent prompts they raise go through someone who reviews them.
checks.blurb: The tenant lets any user create app registrations (should be admin-only).

checks.label: Unrestricted user app-consent
checks.fix: Set User consent for applications to Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions, and enable the admin consent request workflow. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Enterprise apps > Consent and permissions > User consent settings.
checks.impact: Unrestricted user consent is the illicit-consent-grant attack path; one click hands an app access to your data.
checks.best_practice: Users should only be able to consent to apps from verified publishers requesting low-risk permissions, with anything broader routed to an admin; keep the admin consent request workflow switched on so a blocked user still has a clean path to ask.
checks.blurb: Users can consent to apps beyond low-risk permissions, or the admin-consent workflow is off.

checks.label: Guest invite & access not restricted
checks.fix: Set Guest invite settings to Only users assigned to specific admin roles can invite guest users, and Guest user access to restricted to properties and memberships of their own directory objects. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > External Identities > External collaboration settings.
checks.impact: Loose guest settings let external accounts into your tenant and let them read more of your directory than they should.
checks.best_practice: Guest invitations should be limited to admins or designated inviters rather than open to anyone, and guests should be given the most-restricted directory role so they cannot enumerate more of your tenant than their work requires.
checks.blurb: Anyone can invite guests, or guests are not set to the most-restricted access level.

checks.label: User self-service creation privileges
checks.fix: Set Prevent non-admins from creating their own tenants to Yes and Users can create security groups to No; delegate both to admins. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Users > User settings.
checks.impact: Uncontrolled tenant and group creation spawns ungoverned identity islands and access nobody is accountable for.
checks.best_practice: Ordinary users should not be able to spin up new tenants, and security-group creation should be governed rather than open to everyone, so identity and access stay under administrative control.
checks.blurb: Users can create new tenants or security groups (should be delegated to admins).

checks.label: No identity security baseline
checks.fix: Enable Security Defaults (set Security defaults to Enabled), or on Entra ID P1+ create Conditional Access policies that enforce MFA and block legacy auth. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Overview > Properties > Manage security defaults.
checks.impact: With neither Security Defaults nor Conditional Access, nothing stands between a stolen password and your tenant.
checks.best_practice: Every tenant needs at least one baseline protecting sign-in: turn on Security Defaults, or on Entra ID P1 and above build Conditional Access policies that enforce MFA and block legacy authentication, so a stolen password alone is never enough.
checks.blurb: Security Defaults are off AND there are no enabled Conditional Access policies.

checks.label: No MFA-for-all Conditional Access policy
checks.fix: Create an enabled Conditional Access policy: All users (exclude break-glass), All resources, Grant access with Require authentication strength, Multifactor authentication. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: MFA for everyone is the single highest-impact identity control; without it a leaked password is a full account takeover.
checks.best_practice: An enabled Conditional Access policy should require MFA for all users across all cloud apps, excluding only the break-glass accounts; universal MFA is the single control that most reduces account takeover from stolen passwords.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy requires MFA for all users.

checks.label: No MFA-for-admins Conditional Access policy
checks.fix: Create an enabled Conditional Access policy: include Directory roles (the privileged admin roles), All resources, Grant access with Require multifactor authentication. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: Admin accounts are the crown jewels; an admin protected only by a password is one phish from tenant compromise.
checks.best_practice: Directory-role holders should always be challenged for MFA by an enabled Conditional Access policy, since an admin account protected only by a password is one phishing email away from tenant compromise.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy requires MFA for directory-role holders.

checks.label: No policy blocking legacy authentication
checks.fix: Create an enabled Conditional Access policy: All users, All resources, condition Client apps set to Exchange ActiveSync clients and Other clients, access control Block access. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: Legacy authentication bypasses MFA entirely and is the top vector for password-spray attacks; it must be blocked.
checks.best_practice: Legacy authentication protocols cannot present a second factor and should be blocked outright by Conditional Access; they are the main way password-spray attacks slip past MFA.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy blocks legacy/basic-auth clients.

checks.label: No MFA for Azure management
checks.fix: Create an enabled Conditional Access policy: All users (exclude break-glass), target resource Windows Azure Service Management API, Grant access with Require multifactor authentication. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: Reaching the Azure control plane (portal / CLI / ARM) without MFA lets a stolen password change your whole estate.
checks.best_practice: Reaching the Azure control plane (portal, CLI or ARM) should require MFA through Conditional Access, so a stolen password cannot be used to change your Azure estate.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy requires MFA for the Azure management API.

checks.label: No sign-in risk Conditional Access policy
checks.fix: Create an enabled Conditional Access policy: All users, All resources, condition Sign-in risk High and Medium, Grant access with Require multifactor authentication, session Sign-in frequency Every time. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: Entra scores every sign-in for risk, but without a policy acting on that score the detection is written to a report nobody reads while the sign-in succeeds.
checks.best_practice: Require MFA when sign-in risk is medium or high, and block at high risk once you trust the signal. The risk score is only worth the licence if a policy acts on it.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy conditions on sign-in risk.

checks.label: No user risk Conditional Access policy
checks.fix: Create an enabled Conditional Access policy: All users, All resources, condition User risk High, Grant access with Require risk remediation (forces a secure password change). Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy.
checks.impact: A user flagged as compromised keeps working normally until someone notices, which turns a detection Entra already made into an incident it did not prevent.
checks.best_practice: Force a secure password change at high user risk, so a compromised account is remediated by the platform rather than by whoever next reads the report.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy conditions on user risk (a likely-compromised account).

checks.label: Admin MFA does not require an authentication strength
checks.fix: On the Conditional Access policy that includes Directory roles, set Grant access to Require authentication strength and select Phishing-resistant MFA strength. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies.
checks.impact: The generic MFA grant accepts SMS and voice calls, both of which are phishable and SIM-swappable, so an admin protected by it is protected against the wrong attack.
checks.best_practice: Require a phishing-resistant strength (FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based) for directory-role holders. Plain MFA still accepts the factors that modern phishing kits defeat in real time.
checks.blurb: No enabled Conditional Access policy targeting directory roles demands a specific authentication strength (e.g. phishing-resistant).

checks.label: Privileged roles held by on-premises-synced accounts
checks.fix: For each synced admin, remove the directory role assignment and re-grant it to a cloud-only account. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Roles & admins > select role > select user > Remove assignment. CLI: Remove-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleAssignment -UnifiedRoleAssignmentId <id>.
checks.impact: If the on-premises directory is compromised, so is the cloud tenant, and during that incident you cannot trust the very accounts you need to respond with.
checks.best_practice: Give privileged roles to cloud-only accounts. A synced admin makes the on-premises domain a single point of failure for the tenant, and leaves you no clean identity to recover with.
checks.blurb: Directory-role holders whose accounts are synced from on-premises Active Directory.

checks.label: Global Administrator count out of range
checks.fix: Adjust Global Administrator membership to 2-4 accounts, one a cloud-only break-glass account; move the rest to narrower roles or PIM eligibility via Remove assignment. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Roles & admins > Global Administrator.
checks.impact: Too few Global Admins risks lockout with no break-glass; too many multiplies the accounts that can take over everything.
checks.best_practice: Between 2 and 4. Two is the floor because a single Global Admin is a lockout waiting to happen. The second is the break-glass account, cloud-only and excluded from Conditional Access. Beyond four, grant a narrower role instead (Microsoft's guidance is fewer than five permanent Global Admins).
checks.blurb: Fewer than 2 (no break-glass) or more than 4 Global Administrators.

checks.label: Weak authentication methods enabled
checks.fix: Set the SMS and Voice call methods to Disabled in the Authentication methods policy and enable Microsoft Authenticator and Passkey (FIDO2) instead. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Authentication methods > Policies.
checks.impact: SMS and voice codes are phishable and SIM-swappable; leaving them on undercuts your MFA with a weak fallback.
checks.best_practice: Phishable factors like SMS and voice codes should be turned off in the Authentication Methods policy and users moved to the Authenticator app or FIDO2 passkeys, so a weak fallback does not undercut your MFA.
checks.blurb: Phishable SMS or Voice methods are still enabled in the Authentication Methods policy.

checks.label: Low MFA registration coverage
checks.fix: Enable the registration campaign (State: Enabled, target Microsoft Authenticator or Passkey, Limited number of snoozes: Enabled) so unregistered users are nudged to register at sign-in. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Authentication methods > Registration campaign > Edit.
checks.impact: Enforcing MFA is meaningless for users who never registered; the coverage gap is where real account takeover happens.
checks.best_practice: Enforcement only protects people who have actually registered a method, so aim for every member account to be registered for MFA; drive the gap to zero with a registration campaign or combined security information before relying on enforcement policies.
checks.blurb: Member users who are not registered for MFA (enforcement can't protect them).

checks.label: Users flagged at risk
checks.fix: Remediate each at-risk user with Reset password, or Dismiss user risk once investigation confirms no compromise, and enable risk-based Conditional Access for automatic remediation. Portal: Entra admin center > Protection > Identity Protection > Risky users.
checks.impact: A standing at-risk account is an active or imminent compromise sitting in your tenant waiting to be used.
checks.best_practice: No account should sit flagged at risk for long; investigate and remediate each one promptly with a password reset or dismissal, and enable risk-based Conditional Access so obvious compromises are challenged automatically.
checks.blurb: Accounts currently flagged at risk by Microsoft Entra Identity Protection.

checks.label: Stale devices (90+ days)
checks.fix: Disable each device inactive 90+ days, wait a grace period, then delete it; back up BitLocker keys first. Portal: Entra admin center > Entra ID > Devices > All devices. CLI: Update-MgDevice -DeviceId <id> -BodyParameter @{accountEnabled=$false}.
checks.impact: Dormant devices still hold refresh tokens and enrolment; cleaning them up shrinks a forgotten attack surface.
checks.best_practice: Devices inactive beyond about 90 days should be retired rather than left registered, because they still hold refresh tokens; Entra's device cleanup rules can remove them automatically so the list does not grow into a forgotten attack surface.
checks.blurb: Registered or joined devices with no sign-in activity in 90+ days.

checks.label: Standing privileged role assignments
checks.fix: Convert each permanent privileged assignment to PIM-eligible: find it on the role's Active roles tab and select Update (or Remove and re-add as Eligible). Portal: Entra admin center > ID Governance > Privileged Identity Management > Microsoft Entra roles > Roles > select role > Active roles.
checks.impact: Always-on admin rights are always-on risk; privileged roles should be PIM-eligible and activated just-in-time.
checks.best_practice: Privileged roles should be held as PIM-eligible and activated just-in-time, not assigned permanently; the target for standing (always-on) admin assignments is effectively zero, so rights exist only while a task actually needs them.
checks.blurb: Permanent (non-PIM) active assignments to privileged directory roles.

checks.label: Key Vaults not using RBAC authorization
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | where tobool(properties.enableRbacAuthorization) != true | project title=name, detail='Legacy access policies (RBAC auth off)', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each vault, create equivalent RBAC role assignments for every access-policy principal, then switch Permission model to Azure role-based access control. Portal: Azure portal > Key vault > Settings > Properties > Permission model. CLI: az keyvault update -n <vault> -g <rg> --enable-rbac-authorization true.
checks.impact: Legacy vault permissions are coarse and hard to audit; one over-broad policy can expose every secret in the vault.
checks.best_practice: RBAC is the recommended authorisation model for Key Vault because roles are granted at a chosen scope and audited in one place, where access policies are coarse and managed per vault. Move each vault to RBAC and remove the old policies once the equivalent role assignments are in place.
checks.blurb: Key Vaults still using the legacy access-policy model instead of RBAC authorisation.

checks.label: Key Vaults without purge protection
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | where tobool(properties.enablePurgeProtection) != true | project title=name, detail='Purge protection disabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each vault, enable purge protection (irreversible once set) so deleted vaults and objects cannot be purged during the retention window. Portal: Azure portal > Key vault > Settings > Properties. CLI: az keyvault update -n <vault> -g <rg> --enable-purge-protection true.
checks.impact: A deleted vault or key would be gone for good; one mistake or malicious action could permanently destroy the credentials your applications depend on.
checks.best_practice: Purge protection should be on for any vault holding production keys or secrets, so a deleted vault or key stays recoverable for the full retention window and cannot be wiped early by mistake or malice. It cannot be turned off again once set, so leave it off only for genuinely disposable test vaults.
checks.blurb: Key Vaults with purge protection disabled.

checks.label: Key Vaults with weak soft-delete
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | where tobool(properties.enableSoftDelete) != true or toint(properties.softDeleteRetentionInDays) < 90 | project title=name, detail=strcat('Soft-delete retention ', tostring(properties.softDeleteRetentionInDays), 'd'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each vault, enable soft delete and set the retention period to 90 days (the retention interval cannot be changed once saved). Portal: Azure portal > Key vault > Settings > Properties. CLI: az keyvault update -n <vault> -g <rg> --enable-soft-delete true.
checks.impact: A short recovery window turns an accidental deletion into a permanent loss of keys and secrets.
checks.best_practice: Soft-delete should be enabled with the full 90-day retention, which is the maximum window and gives ample time to notice and undo an accidental or malicious deletion before it becomes permanent.
checks.blurb: Key Vaults with soft-delete turned off or a retention window shorter than 90 days.

checks.label: Key Vaults with public network access
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | where tostring(properties.networkAcls.defaultAction) !~ 'Deny' | project title=name, detail='Public network access enabled, no default-deny', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each vault, set up a private endpoint or allow-list known networks (default action Deny), then set Allow access from to Disable public access. Portal: Azure portal > Key vault > Networking > Firewalls and virtual networks. CLI: az keyvault update -n <vault> -g <rg> --public-network-access Disabled.
checks.impact: Your credential store is reachable from the public internet; anyone with a stolen token can try it from anywhere in the world.
checks.best_practice: A credential store should not be open to the whole internet; set the network default action to deny and reach the vault over a private endpoint or an allow-list of known networks, so a stolen token cannot simply be replayed from anywhere.
checks.blurb: Key Vaults reachable from any network, with public access on and no default-deny firewall.

checks.label: Key Vault access policies granting all permissions
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | mv-expand pol=properties.accessPolicies | where pol.permissions.secrets has 'all' or pol.permissions.keys has 'all' or pol.permissions.certificates has 'all' | project title=name, detail=strcat('Principal ', tostring(pol.objectId), ' has All permissions'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id=strcat(tostring(id), '/accessPolicies/', tostring(pol.objectId))
checks.fix: Replace each All-permission access policy with a least-privilege Key Vault RBAC role (e.g. Key Vault Secrets User) for that principal, then move the vault to RBAC. Portal: Azure portal > Key vault > Access control (IAM) > Add role assignment. CLI: az role assignment create --role <KV role> --assignee <id> --scope <vault-id>.
checks.impact: An identity with every vault permission can read, replace, and delete all secrets at once; one compromise empties the vault.
checks.best_practice: Grant only the specific permissions an identity needs rather than the full set, since a wildcard grant lets one compromised principal read, replace, and delete everything in the vault at once. Scoped RBAC roles are preferable to broad access policies.
checks.blurb: Key Vault access policies that grant a principal every permission (All) on secrets, keys, or certificates.

checks.label: Storage accounts allowing public blob access
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | where tobool(properties.allowBlobPublicAccess) == true | project title=name, detail='Blob public access allowed', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each storage account, set Allow Blob anonymous access to Disabled and serve shared data via time-limited SAS or Entra ID instead. Portal: Azure portal > Storage account > Settings > Configuration. CLI: az storage account update -n <account> -g <rg> --allow-blob-public-access false.
checks.impact: Files in these accounts can be opened by anyone on the internet with a link; this is how customer-data leaks make the news.
checks.best_practice: Anonymous blob access should be switched off at the account so no container can be opened without credentials; share data instead through a time-limited SAS or Entra ID (RBAC), which can be scoped and revoked.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts where anonymous public access to blob containers is allowed at the account level.

checks.label: Storage accounts open to all networks
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' and tostring(properties.networkAcls.defaultAction) !~ 'Deny' | project title=name, detail='Public network access, no default-deny', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each storage account, set public network access to Enabled from selected networks (default action Deny) with allow-listed VNets/IPs, or Disable it and use a private endpoint. Portal: Azure portal > Storage account > Security + networking > Networking > Manage. CLI: az storage account update -n <account> -g <rg> --default-action Deny.
checks.impact: Storage that accepts traffic from any network relies on keys alone; a single leaked key means immediate data exposure.
checks.best_practice: Restrict storage to known networks by setting the firewall default to deny and allow-listing specific VNets or IPs, or use a private endpoint, so access does not rest on a leaked key alone.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts that accept traffic from any network, with public access on and no default-deny.

checks.label: Storage accounts allowing TLS below 1.2
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | where tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion) in ('TLS1_0','TLS1_1') or isempty(tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion)) | project title=name, detail=strcat('minimumTlsVersion=', tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each storage account, set Minimum TLS version to Version 1.2. Portal: Azure portal > Storage account > Settings > Configuration > Minimum TLS version. CLI: az storage account update -n <account> -g <rg> --min-tls-version TLS1_2.
checks.impact: Outdated encryption protocols are breakable in transit; data moving to these accounts can be intercepted and read.
checks.best_practice: Require TLS 1.2 as the minimum, since the older versions have known weaknesses that can be broken in transit and 1.2 is Microsoft's current baseline for storage.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts whose minimum TLS version is 1.0, 1.1, or unset.

checks.label: Storage accounts not enforcing HTTPS
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | where tobool(properties.supportsHttpsTrafficOnly) != true | project title=name, detail='HTTP traffic permitted', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each storage account, set Secure transfer required to Enabled so plain-HTTP requests are rejected. Portal: Azure portal > Storage account > Settings > Configuration > Secure transfer required. CLI: az storage account update -n <account> -g <rg> --https-only true.
checks.impact: Data travelling to these accounts can go unencrypted over the wire, readable by anyone in the network path.
checks.best_practice: Enforce HTTPS-only so no data ever crosses the network in clear text where it could be read in the network path; this is the Microsoft default for new accounts.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts that still permit plain HTTP, with secure-transfer-required turned off.

checks.label: Storage accounts allowing shared-key access
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | where isnull(properties.allowSharedKeyAccess) or tobool(properties.allowSharedKeyAccess) == true | project title=name, detail='Shared-key (account key) access enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each storage account, migrate clients to Entra ID or user-delegation SAS, then set Allow storage account key access to Disabled. Portal: Azure portal > Storage account > Settings > Configuration > Allow storage account key access. CLI: az storage account update -n <account> -g <rg> --allow-shared-key-access false.
checks.impact: Account keys grant full access, never expire on their own, and cannot be traced to a person; one leak exposes everything stored.
checks.best_practice: Prefer Entra ID (RBAC) or user-delegation SAS over account keys, because keys grant full access, do not expire on their own, and cannot be tied to a person. Disable shared-key access once every consumer has moved to identity-based auth.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts that still allow shared-key (account key) authentication, or leave the setting unset.

checks.label: Storage accounts without infrastructure encryption
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | where tobool(properties.encryption.requireInfrastructureEncryption) != true | project title=name, detail='Infrastructure (double) encryption off', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Where a regulation requires double encryption, recreate the account with infrastructure encryption enabled (it cannot be turned on after creation) and migrate the data. Portal: Azure portal > Storage accounts > Create > Encryption tab > Enable infrastructure encryption. CLI: az storage account create --require-infrastructure-encryption.
checks.impact: Where regulations demand double encryption at rest, these accounts fall short of that bar.
checks.best_practice: Enable infrastructure encryption only where a regulation or contract calls for a second layer of encryption at rest; for most workloads the default single layer is sufficient, and this option can only be chosen when the account is first created.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts without infrastructure (double) encryption at rest.

checks.label: NSG rules exposing SSH/RDP to the internet
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | mv-expand rule=properties.securityRules | where tostring(rule.properties.direction) =~ 'Inbound' and tostring(rule.properties.access) =~ 'Allow' and tostring(rule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix) in ('*','0.0.0.0/0','Internet') | extend ports=strcat(tostring(rule.properties.destinationPortRange), ' ', strcat_array(todynamic(rule.properties.destinationPortRanges),',')) | where ports has '22' or ports has '3389' or tostring(rule.properties.destinationPortRange) == '*' | project title=name, detail=strcat('Rule ', tostring(rule.name), ' allows ', ports, ' from ', tostring(rule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id=strcat(tostring(id), '/securityRules/', tostring(rule.name))
checks.fix: On each flagged rule, change Source from Any/Internet to your admin CIDRs, or delete it and reach VMs via Azure Bastion or just-in-time access. Portal: Azure portal > Network security groups > [NSG] > Inbound security rules. CLI: az network nsg rule update -g <rg> --nsg-name <nsg> -n <rule> --source-address-prefixes <cidr>.
checks.impact: Remote-admin ports open to the internet are found by scanners within minutes and are the most common way servers get breached.
checks.best_practice: Remote-admin ports should never be open to the whole internet; restrict the source to known addresses, or better, reach servers through Azure Bastion or just-in-time access so the ports stay closed until they are needed.
checks.blurb: NSG inbound rules that allow SSH (22) or RDP (3389) from the internet, meaning a source of any, 0.0.0.0/0, or Internet.

checks.label: NSG rules allowing all inbound traffic from internet
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | mv-expand rule=properties.securityRules | where tostring(rule.properties.direction) =~ 'Inbound' and tostring(rule.properties.access) =~ 'Allow' and tostring(rule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix) in ('*','0.0.0.0/0','Internet') and tostring(rule.properties.destinationPortRange) == '*' | project title=name, detail=strcat('Rule ', tostring(rule.name), ' allows ALL ports from internet'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id=strcat(tostring(id), '/securityRules/', tostring(rule.name))
checks.fix: Replace each any-any allow rule with rules naming only the ports and source ranges the service actually needs, or delete it. Portal: Azure portal > Network security groups > [NSG] > Inbound security rules. CLI: az network nsg rule delete -g <rg> --nsg-name <nsg> -n <rule>.
checks.impact: A rule allowing all traffic from anywhere makes the firewall decorative; every service on those machines is exposed.
checks.best_practice: Inbound rules should name the specific ports and sources a service actually needs; an allow-all-from-anywhere rule defeats the firewall and exposes every port on the attached machines.
checks.blurb: NSG inbound rules that allow every port from the internet, with any source and a destination port of *.

checks.label: Unattached public IPs
checks.kql: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/publicipaddresses' | where tostring(properties.ipConfiguration) == '' and tostring(properties.natGateway) == '' and tostring(properties.publicIPPrefix) == '' | project title=name, detail=strcat('Attached to nothing · ', tostring(sku.name)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each unattached public IP (Standard SKU bills hourly even when idle); if it still shows an association, select Dissociate first. Portal: Azure portal > Public IP addresses > select the IP > Delete. CLI: az network public-ip delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: Each idle address bills hourly and is a door on the internet nobody is watching.
checks.blurb: Public IP addresses attached to no IP configuration, NAT gateway, or public IP prefix.

checks.label: Subnets without a network security group
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | mv-expand sn=properties.subnets | where isnull(sn.properties.networkSecurityGroup) and tostring(sn.name) !in ('GatewaySubnet','AzureBastionSubnet','AzureFirewallSubnet') | project title=strcat(name, '/', tostring(sn.name)), detail='Subnet has no NSG', rtype='microsoft.network/virtualNetworks/subnets', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id=strcat(tostring(id), '/subnets/', tostring(sn.name))
checks.fix: Associate an NSG with each unprotected workload subnet. Portal: Azure portal > Network security groups > [NSG] > Subnets > + Associate. CLI: az network vnet subnet update -g <rg> --vnet-name <vnet> -n <subnet> --network-security-group <nsg>.
checks.impact: Workloads in these network segments have no traffic filter at all; anything that gets in can move sideways freely.
checks.best_practice: Every workload subnet should have an NSG so traffic is filtered by default and a compromised host cannot move freely to its neighbours; the platform-managed gateway, Bastion, and firewall subnets are the intended exceptions.
checks.blurb: Workload subnets with no network security group attached, excluding the gateway, Bastion, and firewall subnets.

checks.label: Unattached managed disks
checks.kql: resources | where type has 'microsoft.compute/disks' | extend ds=tostring(properties.diskState) | where (managedBy == '' and ds != 'ActiveSAS') or (ds == 'Unattached' and ds != 'ActiveSAS') | where not(name endswith '-ASRReplica' or name startswith 'ms-asr-' or name startswith 'asrseeddisk-') | project title=name, detail=strcat('Unattached ', tostring(properties.diskSizeGB), ' GB'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Snapshot each disk if its data may still be needed, confirm Disk state reads Unattached, then delete it (deletion is permanent). Portal: Azure portal > Disks > select the disk > Delete. CLI: az disk delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: You pay monthly for storage no machine uses, and the forgotten data on it still needs protecting.
checks.blurb: Managed disks attached to nothing (Unattached or unmanaged-by-any-resource), excluding ASR replica and seed disks.

checks.label: Managed disks without customer-managed key encryption
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/disks' | where isnull(properties.encryption.type) or tostring(properties.encryption.type) =~ 'EncryptionAtRestWithPlatformKey' | project title=name, detail='Platform-managed key only', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id | take 200
checks.fix: Where compliance requires it, create a disk encryption set, stop the VM, and switch each disk's Key management to the customer-managed key. Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM (stopped) > Disks > disk > Encryption > Key management.
checks.impact: Where compliance requires you to hold your own encryption keys, these disks do not meet that requirement.
checks.best_practice: The platform-managed key is enough for most workloads; move to a customer-managed key only where a regulation or policy requires you to hold and control your own encryption key.
checks.blurb: Managed disks encrypted only with a platform-managed key, with no customer-managed key set.

checks.label: VMs using unmanaged (legacy) disks
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | where isnull(properties.storageProfile.osDisk.managedDisk) | project title=name, detail='OS disk is unmanaged (legacy)', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Migrate each VM to managed disks (the VM is stopped and restarted; migrate any availability set first). Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM > Disks > Migrate to managed disks. CLI: ConvertTo-AzVMManagedDisk -ResourceGroupName <rg> -VMName <vm>.
checks.impact: Legacy disks miss modern reliability and security features and complicate recovery when hardware fails.
checks.best_practice: Move VMs to managed disks, the current standard, which bring the reliability, encryption, and backup features that legacy unmanaged disks lack.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines whose OS disk is still an unmanaged, storage-account-backed disk.

checks.label: Owner role assigned at subscription scope
checks.kql: authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roleassignments' | extend rdef=tostring(properties.roleDefinitionId), scope=tostring(properties.scope) | where rdef endswith '8e3af657-a8ff-443c-a75c-2fe8c4bcb635' | where scope matches regex '^/subscriptions/[^/]+$' | extend subId=tostring(split(scope,'/')[2]) | project title=tostring(properties.principalId), detail=strcat('Owner (', tostring(properties.principalType), ') at subscription scope'), sub=subId, id
checks.fix: Replace each subscription-scope Owner grant with a least-privilege role at the narrowest scope, assigned via a group. Portal: Azure portal > Subscriptions > Access control (IAM) > Role assignments > select assignment > Remove. CLI: Remove-AzRoleAssignment -ObjectId <id> -RoleDefinitionName Owner -Scope /subscriptions/<subId>.
checks.impact: An Owner at subscription level can change anything, including security settings; every extra Owner multiplies what one stolen account can do.
checks.best_practice: Keep subscription Owners to a deliberate few, since Owner can change anything including security controls; grant a narrower role at the smallest scope that does the job, and assign through groups rather than to individuals.
checks.blurb: Principals holding the Owner role assigned directly at subscription scope.

checks.label: Resources without governance tags
checks.kql: resources | where notempty(resourceGroup) | where isnull(tags) or not(bag_keys(tags) has_any ('Environment','environment','Owner','owner','CostCenter','costCenter')) | summarize n=count() by subscriptionId, resourceGroup | project title=resourceGroup, detail=strcat(tostring(n), ' untagged resources'), rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId | take 200
checks.fix: Assign the built-in 'Require a tag on resources' policy for Environment, Owner, and CostCenter (use the modify-effect 'Add a tag to resources' variants with a remediation task to backfill existing resources). Portal: Azure portal > Policy > Definitions > search 'tag' > Assign.
checks.impact: Without ownership tags, nobody can say what a resource is for, who pays for it, or whether it can be switched off.
checks.best_practice: Every resource should carry at least ownership, environment, and cost-centre tags so spend and responsibility can be traced; enforce the set with an Azure Policy require-tag rule rather than relying on people to remember.
checks.blurb: Resources carrying none of the governance tags (Environment, Owner, or CostCenter), counted per resource group.

checks.label: Production VMs not zone-redundant
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | where tostring(tags['Environment']) in~ ('prod','production') | where isnull(zones) or array_length(zones) == 0 | project title=name, detail='Production VM not in an availability zone', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Move each production VM into an availability zone (the move stops the source VM and creates a zonal copy in the same region). Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM > Availability + scaling > Edit > Target availability zone.
checks.impact: A single datacenter issue would take these production machines down; zone redundancy keeps them running through it.
checks.best_practice: Spread production machines across availability zones, or at least an availability set, so a single datacentre fault does not take the workload down; zone placement is what raises the single-instance availability commitment.
checks.blurb: Production-tagged VMs that are not placed in any availability zone.

checks.label: Tag governance: untagged resources
checks.kql: resources | where notempty(resourceGroup) | where isnull(tags) or array_length(bag_keys(tags)) == 0 | summarize n=count() by subscriptionId | join kind=leftouter (resourcecontainers | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions' | project subscriptionId, subName=name) on subscriptionId | project title=coalesce(subName, subscriptionId), detail=strcat(tostring(n), ' resources have no tags at all'), sub=subscriptionId
checks.fix: Assign the built-in tag policies for your taxonomy (Require a tag on resources to block new gaps, Add a tag to resources with a remediation task to backfill existing ones). Portal: Azure portal > Policy > Definitions > search Tags > Assign.
checks.impact: An untagged estate makes cost allocation and ownership guesswork, so waste and risk go unclaimed.
checks.best_practice: Adopt a small, consistent tagging taxonomy and apply it across the estate so cost, ownership, and environment can be reported on; enforcing it through Azure Policy keeps new resources compliant automatically.
checks.blurb: Resources with no tags at all, counted per subscription.

checks.label: Empty resource groups
checks.kql: resourcecontainers | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions/resourcegroups' | join kind=leftouter (resources | summarize c=count() by resourceGroup, subscriptionId) on resourceGroup, subscriptionId | where isnull(c) | project title=name, detail='Empty resource group', sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each empty resource group. Portal: Azure portal > Resource groups > select group > Delete resource group. CLI: Remove-AzResourceGroup -Name <rg>.
checks.impact: Empty groups accumulate as clutter that slows audits and hides real changes.
checks.blurb: Resource groups that contain no resources.

checks.label: Subscriptions with Defender for Cloud on Free tier
checks.kql: securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/pricings' | where tostring(properties.pricingTier) =~ 'Free' | summarize plans=make_set(name) by subscriptionId | join kind=leftouter (resourcecontainers | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions' | project subscriptionId, subName=name) on subscriptionId | project title=coalesce(subName, subscriptionId), detail=strcat('Defender Free tier on: ', strcat_array(plans, ', ')), sub=subscriptionId
checks.fix: On each subscription, switch the listed Defender for Cloud plans from Free to On for the resource types you run. Portal: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > [subscription] > toggle plans On > Save. CLI: Set-AzSecurityPricing -Name <plan> -PricingTier Standard.
checks.impact: These subscriptions run without Microsoft's threat detection; an attack in progress would go unnoticed.
checks.best_practice: Turn on Defender for Cloud's paid plans for the resource types you run, so active threats are actually detected; the free tier gives you the secure-score recommendations but none of the threat protection.
checks.blurb: Subscriptions where one or more Defender for Cloud plans are still on the Free tier.

checks.label: App Service plans with no apps
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/serverfarms' | where toint(properties.numberOfSites) == 0 | project title=name, detail=strcat('Hosts 0 apps · ', tostring(sku.name)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each App Service plan hosting zero apps, or move it to the Free tier if you intend to reuse it; empty plans still bill for their reserved instances. Portal: Azure portal > App Service plans > select the plan > Delete. CLI: az appservice plan delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: These plans bill every hour while hosting nothing at all.
checks.blurb: App Service plans hosting zero apps.

checks.label: Availability sets not associated to any VM
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/availabilitySets' | where tostring(properties.virtualMachines) == '[]' | where not(name endswith '-asr') | project title=name, detail='No VMs associated', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each availability set with no VMs associated; an empty set is dead configuration and can be removed safely. Portal: Azure portal > Availability sets > select the set > Delete. CLI: az vm availability-set delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: Leftovers from deleted machines; harmless to remove, and every one gone makes the estate easier to audit.
checks.blurb: Availability sets with no virtual machines associated, excluding ASR-suffixed sets.

checks.label: Dangling network interfaces
checks.kql: resources | where type has 'microsoft.network/networkinterfaces' | where isnull(properties.privateEndpoint) and isnull(properties.privateLinkService) | where tostring(properties.hostedWorkloads) == '[]' and properties !has 'virtualmachine' | project title=name, detail='Attached to nothing', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each dangling network interface (a NIC not attached to a VM, private endpoint, or private link service can be deleted directly). Portal: Azure portal > Network interfaces > select the NIC > Delete. CLI: az network nic delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: Leftover network parts from deleted machines clutter audits and hide the changes that actually matter.
checks.blurb: Network interfaces attached to nothing, with no VM, private endpoint, or private link service.

checks.label: Unattached network security groups
checks.kql: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' and isnull(properties.networkInterfaces) and isnull(properties.subnets) | project title=name, detail='Not attached to any NIC or subnet', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each NSG not associated to any NIC or subnet; unattached NSGs cost nothing but add clutter and audit noise. Portal: Azure portal > Network security groups > select the NSG > Delete. CLI: az network nsg delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: Unused firewalls cost nothing but make every security review slower and noisier.
checks.blurb: Network security groups not attached to any NIC or subnet.

checks.label: Unattached route tables
checks.kql: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/routetables' | where isnull(properties.subnets) | project title=name, detail='Not attached to any subnet', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each route table not associated to any subnet. Portal: Azure portal > Route tables > select the table > Delete. CLI: az network route-table delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: Leftover routing rules sit waiting to cause confusion the next time someone attaches them.
checks.blurb: Route tables not attached to any subnet.

checks.label: Traffic Manager profiles without endpoints
checks.kql: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/trafficmanagerprofiles' | where tostring(properties.endpoints) == '[]' | project title=name, detail='No endpoints', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each Traffic Manager profile with no endpoints, after confirming no DNS CNAME record still points at its domain name. Portal: Azure portal > Traffic Manager profiles > select the profile > Overview > Delete. CLI: Remove-AzTrafficManagerProfile -Name <name> -ResourceGroupName <rg>.
checks.impact: Profiles with no destinations serve no traffic but still bill for every lookup.
checks.blurb: Traffic Manager profiles whose endpoint list is empty.

checks.label: Virtual networks without subnets
checks.kql: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | where tostring(properties.subnets) == '[]' | project title=name, detail='No subnets', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each virtual network with no subnets; check Connected devices is empty, then remove it. Portal: Azure portal > Virtual networks > select the network > Delete. CLI: az network vnet delete -g <rg> -n <name>.
checks.impact: Empty networks are clutter that makes the real network layout harder to review.
checks.blurb: Virtual networks that contain no subnets.

checks.label: SQL elastic pools without databases
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers/elasticpools' | extend epId=tolower(id) | join kind=leftouter (resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers/databases' | extend epId=tolower(tostring(properties.elasticPoolId)) | where epId != '' | distinct epId | extend hasdb=1) on epId | where isnull(hasdb) | project title=name, detail='0 databases in pool', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Delete each elastic pool holding zero databases (it bills for its full reserved capacity regardless), or repurpose it by moving databases in via Configure pool. Portal: Azure portal > SQL elastic pools > select the pool > Delete. CLI: az sql elastic-pool delete -g <rg> -s <server> -n <pool>.
checks.impact: You pay for reserved database capacity that hosts no databases at all.
checks.best_practice: An elastic pool earns its reserved cost only when it holds several databases whose demand is spread out; if it hosts none, retire it, and if it hosts one, move that database to a standalone tier that bills for what it uses.
checks.blurb: SQL elastic pools that no database is assigned to.

checks.label: SQL servers reachable over the public network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | project title=name, detail='Public network access enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each SQL logical server, set Public network access to Disabled and connect via private endpoints. Portal: Azure portal > SQL server > Security > Networking > Public access. CLI: az sql server update -n <server> -g <rg> --set publicNetworkAccess=Disabled.
checks.impact: A database server reachable from the public internet is the single highest-value target for data theft and brute-force attacks.
checks.best_practice: Keep public network access disabled and reach the server over a private endpoint or VNet rule, so the database is never addressable from the open internet. Where a public path is genuinely required, scope it to named IPs rather than leaving the door open to everyone.
checks.blurb: SQL servers whose public network access is set to Enabled.

checks.label: SQL server firewall open to the whole internet
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers/firewallrules' | where tostring(properties.startIpAddress) == '0.0.0.0' and tostring(properties.endIpAddress) == '255.255.255.255' | project title=tostring(split(id,'/')[8]), detail=strcat('Firewall rule ', tostring(name), ' allows 0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255'), rtype='microsoft.sql/servers', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each SQL server, delete the firewall rule spanning 0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255 and allow only the specific client IPs that need access. Portal: Azure portal > SQL server > Security > Networking > Public access > Firewall rules. CLI: az sql server firewall-rule delete -g <rg> -s <server> -n <rule>.
checks.impact: A firewall rule spanning every address leaves the database open to the entire internet, negating network protection.
checks.best_practice: A firewall rule should allow only the specific addresses that need to connect; an any-to-any rule is the same as having no firewall at all. Prefer private endpoints, and where public access is needed pin it to individual hosts or small ranges.
checks.blurb: SQL server firewall rules that span the entire IPv4 range from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255.

checks.label: SQL servers without a Microsoft Entra admin
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers' | where isnull(properties.administrators) or isempty(tostring(properties.administrators.login)) | project title=name, detail='No Microsoft Entra admin configured', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each SQL server, set a Microsoft Entra admin, preferably a group. Portal: Azure portal > SQL server > Settings > Microsoft Entra ID > Set admin. CLI: Set-AzSqlServerActiveDirectoryAdministrator -ResourceGroupName <rg> -ServerName <server> -DisplayName <group>.
checks.impact: Without an Entra admin the database can only be governed by SQL logins, outside your central identity and MFA controls.
checks.best_practice: Every SQL server should have an Entra administrator set, ideally a group rather than a single person, so database access is governed by your central identity, Conditional Access, and MFA instead of standalone SQL logins.
checks.blurb: SQL servers with no Microsoft Entra administrator configured.

checks.label: SQL servers still allowing SQL authentication
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers' | where isnull(properties.administrators.azureADOnlyAuthentication) or tobool(properties.administrators.azureADOnlyAuthentication) != true | project title=name, detail='Microsoft Entra-only authentication not enforced', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each SQL server with an Entra admin set, check Support only Microsoft Entra authentication for this server to disable SQL password logins. Portal: Azure portal > SQL server > Settings > Microsoft Entra ID. CLI: az sql server ad-only-auth enable -g <rg> -n <server>.
checks.impact: SQL-authentication passwords sit outside conditional access and MFA, so one leaked connection string is a direct way in.
checks.best_practice: Once an Entra admin is in place, turn on Entra-only authentication so password-based SQL logins are switched off entirely; that removes the leaked-connection-string risk and brings every login under Conditional Access and MFA.
checks.blurb: SQL servers that have not enforced Microsoft Entra-only authentication (password SQL logins still permitted).

checks.label: Cosmos DB accounts allowing key-based (local) auth
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts' | where isnull(properties.disableLocalAuth) or tobool(properties.disableLocalAuth) != true | project title=name, detail='Key-based (local) authentication is enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each Cosmos DB account, set disableLocalAuth to true and grant data access via Microsoft Entra RBAC roles instead of account keys. Portal: not exposed for this setting, use the CLI. CLI: az resource update -g <rg> -n <account> --resource-type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts --set properties.disableLocalAuth=true.
checks.impact: Shared account keys bypass Entra RBAC entirely and cannot be attributed or individually revoked when leaked.
checks.best_practice: Disable local authentication and grant data access through Entra RBAC roles, so each caller has an identity that can be attributed and revoked individually. Shared account keys should be a break-glass fallback at most, not the everyday path.
checks.blurb: Cosmos DB accounts that still allow key-based (local) authentication.

checks.label: Cosmos DB accounts allowing key-based metadata writes
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts' | where isnull(properties.disableKeyBasedMetadataWriteAccess) or tobool(properties.disableKeyBasedMetadataWriteAccess) != true | project title=name, detail='Key-based metadata write access not disabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each Cosmos DB account, set disableKeyBasedMetadataWriteAccess to true so container and throughput changes require an Entra identity. Portal: not exposed for this setting, use the CLI. CLI: az cosmosdb update -g <rg> -n <account> --disable-key-based-metadata-write-access true.
checks.impact: With key-based metadata writes on, anyone holding an account key can reshape the database, not just read data.
checks.best_practice: Turn off key-based metadata writes so that changing containers, throughput, and other structure requires an Entra identity with the right role; that confines account keys to data operations and keeps configuration changes attributable.
checks.blurb: Cosmos DB accounts that still allow key-based metadata write operations.

checks.label: PostgreSQL flexible servers open to the public network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.dbforpostgresql/flexibleservers' | where tostring(properties.network.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | project title=name, detail='Public network access enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each PostgreSQL flexible server, clear the Allow public access to this resource through the internet using a public IP address checkbox and connect via private endpoints. Portal: Azure portal > PostgreSQL flexible server > Settings > Networking. CLI: az postgres flexible-server update -g <rg> -n <server> --public-access disabled.
checks.impact: A publicly reachable PostgreSQL endpoint is directly attackable from anywhere on the internet.
checks.best_practice: Run the server on private (VNet-integrated) access with public network access disabled, so the database endpoint is not reachable from the internet. Reserve any public exposure for narrowly allow-listed addresses.
checks.blurb: PostgreSQL flexible servers whose public network access is Enabled.

checks.label: MySQL flexible servers open to the public network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.dbformysql/flexibleservers' | where tostring(properties.network.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | project title=name, detail='Public network access enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each MySQL flexible server, clear the Allow public access to this resource through the internet using a public IP address checkbox and connect via private endpoints. Portal: Azure portal > MySQL flexible server > Settings > Networking.
checks.impact: A publicly reachable MySQL endpoint is directly attackable from anywhere on the internet.
checks.best_practice: Run the server on private (VNet-integrated) access with public network access disabled, so the database endpoint is not reachable from the internet. Reserve any public exposure for narrowly allow-listed addresses.
checks.blurb: MySQL flexible servers whose public network access is Enabled.

checks.label: Defender for Cloud not enabled on database plans
checks.kql: securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/pricings' | where name in~ ('SqlServers','SqlServerVirtualMachines','OpenSourceRelationalDatabases','CosmosDbs') | where tostring(properties.pricingTier) !~ 'Standard' | project title=name, detail=strcat(tostring(name), ' plan is on the Free tier'), sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each subscription hosting data, switch the Defender for Cloud Databases plan to On (covers SQL, SQL on VM, open-source DBs and Cosmos). Portal: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > subscription > Defender plans > Databases. CLI: Set-AzSecurityPricing -Name SqlServers -PricingTier Standard.
checks.impact: Without Defender for databases you get no native threat detection or vulnerability assessment on your data tier.
checks.best_practice: Enable the paid Defender for Cloud database plans on every subscription that hosts data, so the data tier gets native threat detection and vulnerability assessment rather than being a blind spot. The per-resource cost is small next to a database breach.
checks.blurb: Subscriptions whose Defender for Cloud database plans (SQL, SQL-on-VM, open-source DBs, Cosmos) are still on the Free tier.

checks.label: Container registries with weak access controls
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerregistry/registries' | where tobool(properties.adminUserEnabled) == true or tobool(properties.anonymousPullEnabled) == true | project title=name, detail=strcat('adminUser=', tostring(properties.adminUserEnabled), ' anonymousPull=', tostring(properties.anonymousPullEnabled)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each registry, disable the admin user and turn anonymous pull off so only Entra identities can authenticate. Portal: Azure portal > Container registry > Settings > Access keys (uncheck Admin user). CLI: az acr update -n <registry> --admin-enabled false --anonymous-pull-enabled false.
checks.impact: The ACR admin account is a shared password that bypasses identity, and anonymous pull leaks your private images.
