checks.best_practice: Disable the ACR admin account and anonymous pull, and authenticate to the registry with Entra identities and tokens; that gives per-user access you can attribute and revoke, and keeps private images from being pulled by anyone.
checks.blurb: Container registries with the admin account enabled or anonymous pull turned on.

checks.label: Redis caches allowing non-TLS access
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.cache/redis' | where tobool(properties.enableNonSslPort) == true or tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion) != '1.2' | project title=name, detail=strcat('nonSslPort=', tostring(properties.enableNonSslPort), ' minTls=', tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each cache, set Allow access only via SSL to Yes and Minimum TLS version to 1.2. Portal: Azure portal > Azure Cache for Redis > Settings > Advanced settings. CLI: Set-AzRedisCache -Name <cache> -MinimumTlsVersion '1.2'.
checks.impact: The plaintext Redis port and legacy TLS expose cached data and keys to interception in transit.
checks.best_practice: Keep the non-TLS port closed and require TLS 1.2 or higher, so cached data and access keys are never carried in clear text or over a broken protocol version.
checks.blurb: Redis caches with the non-SSL port enabled or a minimum TLS version below 1.2.

checks.label: Service Bus / Event Hub namespaces allowing SAS (local) auth
checks.kql: resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.servicebus/namespaces','microsoft.eventhub/namespaces') | where isnull(properties.disableLocalAuth) or tobool(properties.disableLocalAuth) != true | project title=name, detail='SAS-key (local) authentication is enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each namespace, set Local Authentication to Disabled after moving clients to Entra RBAC data roles. Portal: Azure portal > Service Bus or Event Hubs namespace > Overview > Local Authentication. CLI: az servicebus namespace update -g <rg> -n <namespace> --disable-local-auth true.
checks.impact: SAS access keys grant messaging access outside Entra, so a leaked key cannot be traced or centrally revoked.
checks.best_practice: Disable local (SAS-key) authentication and use Entra RBAC for messaging access, so each sender and receiver has an identity that can be traced and revoked rather than a shared key that cannot.
checks.blurb: Service Bus or Event Hub namespaces that still allow SAS-key (local) authentication.

checks.label: App Services not enforcing HTTPS-only
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites' | where tobool(properties.httpsOnly) != true | project title=name, detail='HTTPS-only is disabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, set HTTPS Only to On so all HTTP requests redirect to HTTPS. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Configuration > General settings > HTTPS Only. CLI: az webapp update -g <rg> -n <app> --set httpsOnly=true
checks.impact: Serving an app over plain HTTP lets session tokens and credentials be read or tampered with in transit.
checks.best_practice: Enable HTTPS-only so every HTTP request is redirected to TLS; that protects session tokens and credentials in transit and is a no-cost setting with no downside for a modern client.
checks.blurb: App Services and Function Apps that do not have HTTPS-only enabled.

checks.label: App Services allowing TLS below 1.2
checks.kql: appserviceresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites/config' and id !contains '/slots/' | extend mtls=tostring(properties.MinTlsVersion) | where isnotempty(mtls) and mtls in ('1.0','1.1') | project title=tostring(split(id,'/')[8]), detail=strcat('Minimum TLS ', mtls), rtype='microsoft.web/sites', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, set Minimum Inbound TLS Version (and SCM Minimum Inbound TLS Version) to 1.2 or higher. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Configuration > General settings. CLI: az webapp config set -g <rg> -n <app> --min-tls-version 1.2
checks.impact: TLS 1.0/1.1 are broken protocols; allowing them exposes traffic to downgrade and interception attacks.
checks.best_practice: Set the minimum inbound TLS version to 1.2 or higher, because TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated and vulnerable to downgrade and interception; move to 1.3 where every client supports it.
checks.blurb: App Services whose minimum inbound TLS version is set below 1.2.

checks.label: App Services allowing plain FTP deployment
checks.kql: appserviceresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites/config' and id !contains '/slots/' | where tostring(properties.FtpsState) =~ 'AllAllowed' | project title=tostring(split(id,'/')[8]), detail='Plain FTP deployment allowed (ftpsState=AllAllowed)', rtype='microsoft.web/sites', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, set FTP state to FTPS only, or Disabled if you deploy another way. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Configuration > General settings > Platform settings > FTP state. CLI: az webapp config set -g <rg> -n <app> --ftps-state FtpsOnly
checks.impact: Plain FTP ships deployment credentials and source code across the network in clear text.
checks.best_practice: Set the deployment channel to FTPS-only, or disable FTP entirely if you deploy another way, so publishing credentials and source are never sent in clear text.
checks.blurb: App Services whose FTP deployment state allows plain (non-encrypted) FTP.

checks.label: App Services with remote debugging enabled
checks.kql: appserviceresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites/config' and id !contains '/slots/' | where tobool(properties.RemoteDebuggingEnabled) == true | project title=tostring(split(id,'/')[8]), detail='Remote debugging is enabled', rtype='microsoft.web/sites', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, turn Remote debugging Off; re-enable only briefly for a live diagnosis. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Configuration > General settings > Debugging.
checks.impact: Remote debugging leaves an interactive attach surface into a running production app.
checks.best_practice: Leave remote debugging off on anything running production traffic; enable it only briefly for a live diagnosis and switch it back off, so there is no standing interactive attach point into the app.
checks.blurb: App Services with remote debugging enabled.

checks.label: App Services without a managed identity
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites' | where isnull(identity) or tostring(identity.type) =~ 'None' | project title=name, detail='No managed identity assigned', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, enable a system-assigned managed identity (Status On) and use it for Key Vault and downstream auth instead of secrets in app settings. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Identity > System assigned. CLI: az webapp identity assign -g <rg> -n <app>
checks.impact: Without a managed identity, downstream credentials tend to live as plaintext app settings that never rotate.
checks.best_practice: Assign a managed identity and reach downstream services and Key Vault through it, so there are no static secrets sitting in app settings to leak or forget to rotate. The platform handles the credential lifecycle for you.
checks.blurb: App Services with no managed identity assigned.

checks.label: App Services without HTTP/2 enabled
checks.kql: appserviceresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites/config' and id !contains '/slots/' | where tobool(properties.Http20Enabled) != true | project title=tostring(split(id,'/')[8]), detail='HTTP/2 is not enabled', rtype='microsoft.web/sites', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, set HTTP version to 2.0 under Platform settings. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Configuration > General settings > Platform settings > HTTP version.
checks.impact: Staying on HTTP/1.1 leaves measurable latency and connection-efficiency gains on the table.
checks.best_practice: Turn HTTP/2 on for better connection multiplexing and lower latency; it is a free platform toggle with no application change required.
checks.blurb: App Services that do not have HTTP/2 enabled.

checks.label: Virtual machines not protected by Azure Backup
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | extend vmId=tolower(id) | join kind=leftouter (recoveryservicesresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.recoveryservices/vaults/backupfabrics/protectioncontainers/protecteditems' | extend vmId=tolower(tostring(properties.sourceResourceId)) | project vmId, protected=1) on vmId | where isnull(protected) | project title=name, detail='No Azure Backup protected item found', rtype='microsoft.compute/virtualmachines', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each VM, enable Azure Backup: pick or create a Recovery Services vault, choose a backup policy with retention matching your recovery needs, then select Enable Backup. Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM > Backup.
checks.impact: An unbacked VM has no restore point after ransomware, corruption, or accidental deletion, the most common gap found in a recovery review.
checks.best_practice: Every stateful VM should be covered by an Azure Backup policy with a retention schedule that matches how far back you would need to recover; without a restore point there is no way back from ransomware, corruption, or an accidental delete.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines with no matching protected item in any Recovery Services Vault.

checks.label: Virtual machines without encryption at host
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | where isnull(properties.securityProfile.encryptionAtHost) or tobool(properties.securityProfile.encryptionAtHost) != true | project title=name, detail='Encryption at host is not enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Register the EncryptionAtHost feature (Microsoft.Compute) on the subscription, then deallocate each VM and set Encryption at host to Yes. Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM (deallocated) > Disks > Additional settings > Encryption at host.
checks.impact: Disk encryption alone leaves the temp disk and host cache traffic unencrypted; encryption at host closes that gap.
checks.best_practice: Enable encryption at host so the temporary disk and the disk-to-host cache traffic are encrypted as well, closing the gap that OS and data-disk encryption alone leaves open.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines that do not have encryption at host enabled.

checks.label: Virtual machines without endpoint protection
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | extend vmId=tolower(id) | join kind=leftouter (resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines/extensions' | where tostring(properties.type) in~ ('IaaSAntimalware','MDE.Windows','MDE.Linux','AzureSecurityLinuxAgent','AzureSecurityWindowsAgent') | extend vmId=tolower(substring(id, 0, indexof(id, '/extensions/'))) | project vmId, hasEp=1) on vmId | where isnull(hasEp) | project title=name, detail='No anti-malware / endpoint-protection extension found', rtype='microsoft.compute/virtualmachines', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Enable the Defender for Servers plan so Defender for Endpoint deploys to every VM. Portal: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > subscription > Defender plans > Servers: On. CLI: az security pricing create -n VirtualMachines --tier standard.
checks.impact: A VM with no endpoint protection has no on-host detection or blocking when an attacker lands on it.
checks.best_practice: Every VM should run endpoint protection, ideally Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, so there is on-host detection and blocking the moment an attacker reaches the machine rather than only network-level visibility.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines with no anti-malware or Defender for Endpoint agent extension installed.

checks.label: Virtual machines with a direct public IP
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkinterfaces' | where isnotempty(tostring(properties.virtualMachine.id)) | mv-expand ipc=properties.ipConfigurations | where isnotempty(tostring(ipc.properties.publicIPAddress.id)) | project title=tostring(split(tostring(properties.virtualMachine.id),'/')[-1]), detail='VM network interface has a direct public IP', rtype='microsoft.compute/virtualmachines', rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id=tostring(properties.virtualMachine.id)
checks.fix: On each VM, dissociate the public IP from its NIC and connect through Azure Bastion, a load balancer, or a VPN instead. Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > [VM] > Overview > select the public IP > Dissociate. CLI: az network nic ip-config update -g <rg> --nic-name <nic> -n <ipconfig> --public-ip-address null.
checks.impact: A VM with its own public IP bypasses your network chokepoints and is directly scannable and attackable from the internet.
checks.best_practice: Reach VMs through Azure Bastion, a load balancer, or a VPN rather than a public IP on the NIC, so management traffic passes your network chokepoints and the machine is not directly scannable from the internet.
checks.blurb: Virtual machine network interfaces that have a public IP directly attached.

checks.label: Virtual machines without a managed identity
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | where isnull(identity) or tostring(identity.type) =~ 'None' | project title=name, detail='No managed identity assigned', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each VM, enable the system-assigned managed identity (Status: On, then Save). Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM > Security > Identity > System assigned > Status: On. CLI: az vm identity assign -g <rg> -n <vm>.
checks.impact: Without a managed identity, apps on the VM tend to hold long-lived secrets to reach other Azure services.
checks.best_practice: Give the VM a managed identity so workloads on it authenticate to Azure services without storing long-lived secrets locally; the platform rotates the credential and there is nothing on disk to steal.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines with no managed identity assigned.

checks.label: Storage accounts on locally-redundant storage (LRS)
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageaccounts' | where tostring(sku.name) endswith 'LRS' | project title=name, detail=strcat('Redundancy ', tostring(sku.name), ' (no zone/geo replication)'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each stateful storage account, change the Redundancy setting from LRS to ZRS or GRS/GZRS (zone changes run as a no-downtime conversion). Portal: Azure portal > Storage accounts > account > Data management > Redundancy. CLI: az storage account update -n <name> -g <rg> --sku Standard_GRS.
checks.impact: LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter only; a zone or region loss takes the data with it.
checks.best_practice: For data you cannot easily recreate, choose zone-redundant (ZRS) or geo-redundant (GRS/GZRS) storage so a single datacenter or region loss does not take the data with it; LRS is fine only for data that is transient or reproducible.
checks.blurb: Storage accounts whose SKU redundancy ends in LRS (locally-redundant only).

checks.label: Single-instance VMs with no availability SLA
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | where (isnull(zones) or array_length(zones) == 0) and isempty(tostring(properties.availabilitySet.id)) and isempty(tostring(properties.virtualMachineScaleSet.id)) | project title=name, detail='No availability zone, availability set, or scale set (no uptime SLA)', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Give each production VM a financially backed SLA by moving it into an availability zone (or place it in an availability set or scale set). Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM > Availability + scaling > Edit > Target availability zone.
checks.impact: A lone VM outside a zone or set carries no uptime SLA, so routine host maintenance is a customer-visible outage.
checks.best_practice: Give a production VM a financially-backed uptime SLA by placing it in an availability zone, an availability set, or a scale set; a lone VM has no SLA, so routine host maintenance becomes a visible outage. Two or more instances across zones is the stronger target.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines that sit in no availability zone, availability set, or scale set.

checks.label: Premium SQL databases without zone redundancy
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers/databases' | where tostring(properties.currentSku.tier) in ('Premium','BusinessCritical') | where tobool(properties.zoneRedundant) != true | project title=name, detail=strcat('Zone redundancy off on ', tostring(properties.currentSku.tier), ' tier'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each Premium or Business Critical database, set the zone redundant option to Yes (included at these tiers, online operation). Portal: Azure portal > SQL databases > database > Settings > Compute + Storage. CLI: az sql db update -g <rg> -s <server> -n <db> --zone-redundant.
checks.impact: Premium tiers include zone redundancy for free; leaving it off forfeits the higher SLA at no saving.
checks.best_practice: Turn on zone redundancy for Premium and Business Critical databases; it is included at those tiers, so leaving it off forfeits the higher availability SLA at no saving.
checks.blurb: Premium or Business Critical SQL databases that do not have zone redundancy enabled.

checks.label: Premium App Service plans without zone redundancy
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/serverfarms' | where tostring(sku.tier) in ('PremiumV2','PremiumV3') and toint(sku.capacity) >= 2 | where tobool(properties.zoneRedundant) != true | project title=name, detail=strcat('Zone redundancy off (', tostring(sku.tier), ', capacity ', tostring(sku.capacity), ')'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each multi-instance Premium plan, enable Zone redundancy (requires 2+ instances on a scale unit whose maximum available zones is above 1). Portal: Azure portal > App Service plans > plan > Settings > Scale out (App Service plan) > Zone redundancy. CLI: az appservice plan update -g <rg> -n <plan> --set zoneRedundant=true.
checks.impact: A multi-instance Premium plan without zone spread gets no zone-fault protection despite paying for the instances.
checks.best_practice: Spread a multi-instance Premium plan across availability zones so the instances you are already paying for actually survive a zone fault; without it the extra capacity buys no zone resilience.
checks.blurb: Premium v2/v3 App Service plans running two or more instances without zone redundancy.

checks.label: Basic-SKU public IPs and load balancers (retiring)
checks.kql: resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.network/publicipaddresses','microsoft.network/loadbalancers') | where tostring(sku.name) =~ 'Basic' | project title=name, detail='Basic SKU (no zone redundancy, being retired)', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Upgrade each Basic public IP to Standard: set allocation to static, disassociate it, then use the upgrade banner; migrate Basic load balancers to Standard. Portal: Azure portal > Public IP addresses > IP > Overview > upgrade banner. CLI: az network public-ip update -g <rg> -n <ip> --sku Standard.
checks.impact: Basic public IPs and load balancers have no zone redundancy and are on a retirement path, so they are a reliability and roadmap risk.
checks.best_practice: Move Basic public IPs and load balancers to the Standard SKU ahead of the Basic retirement; Standard adds zone redundancy and secure-by-default behaviour, and migrating on your own schedule is far cheaper than a forced cutover.
checks.blurb: Basic-SKU public IP addresses and load balancers.

checks.label: AKS clusters without Entra / RBAC integration
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' | where isnull(properties.aadProfile) or tobool(properties.enableRBAC) != true | project title=name, detail='No Microsoft Entra integration or Kubernetes RBAC disabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Enable Microsoft Entra integration with Kubernetes RBAC on the cluster, granting access via an Entra admin group. Portal: Azure portal > Kubernetes service > Settings > Security configuration. CLI: az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --enable-aad --aad-admin-group-object-ids <group-id>.
checks.impact: Without Entra and RBAC, cluster access falls back to a shared static admin credential with no per-user identity or MFA.
checks.best_practice: Run AKS with Entra integration and Kubernetes RBAC on, so cluster access is tied to named users and groups under Conditional Access and MFA instead of a shared static admin credential.
checks.blurb: AKS clusters with no Entra profile or with Kubernetes RBAC disabled.

checks.label: AKS clusters with an unrestricted public API server
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' | where tobool(properties.apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster) != true and array_length(properties.apiServerAccessProfile.authorizedIPRanges) == 0 | project title=name, detail='Public API server with no authorized IP ranges', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Set API server authorized IP ranges to known admin and egress IPs, or make the cluster private. Portal: Azure portal > Kubernetes service > Settings > Networking > Resource settings > Manage > Authorized IP ranges. CLI: az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --api-server-authorized-ip-ranges <cidr>.
checks.impact: A world-reachable Kubernetes API server with no IP allow-list is a critical, directly-attackable exposure.
checks.best_practice: Make the cluster private, or at minimum restrict the API server to known IP ranges, so the Kubernetes control plane is not reachable and attackable from the whole internet.
checks.blurb: AKS clusters that are not private and have no authorized IP ranges on the API server.

checks.label: AKS clusters without a network policy
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' | where isempty(tostring(properties.networkProfile.networkPolicy)) or tostring(properties.networkProfile.networkPolicy) =~ 'none' | project title=name, detail='No pod network policy configured', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Install a network policy engine (Cilium recommended) on each cluster, then define default-deny pod policies. Portal: Azure portal > Kubernetes service > Settings > Networking (shows the engine; install is CLI-only). CLI: az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --network-policy azure.
checks.impact: With no network policy every pod can talk to every other pod, so one compromised container can move laterally at will.
checks.best_practice: Enable a network policy (Azure, Calico, or Cilium) and default to denying pod-to-pod traffic, so a single compromised container cannot move laterally across the cluster unchecked.
checks.blurb: AKS clusters with no pod network policy configured (unset or set to none).

checks.label: AKS clusters without an auto-upgrade channel
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' | where isempty(tostring(properties.autoUpgradeProfile.upgradeChannel)) or tostring(properties.autoUpgradeProfile.upgradeChannel) =~ 'none' | project title=name, detail='No auto-upgrade channel set', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Set the cluster auto-upgrade channel to patch or stable and pair it with a maintenance window. Portal: Azure portal > Kubernetes service > Settings > Upgrades > Upgrade version > Automatic upgrade. CLI: az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --auto-upgrade-channel patch.
checks.impact: Clusters with no upgrade channel drift onto unsupported, unpatched Kubernetes versions.
checks.best_practice: Set an auto-upgrade channel such as patch or stable so the cluster stays on a supported, patched Kubernetes version instead of drifting out of support; pair it with a maintenance window to control when upgrades land.
checks.blurb: AKS clusters with no auto-upgrade channel set (unset or none).

checks.label: Log Analytics workspaces with short retention
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.operationalinsights/workspaces' | where toint(properties.retentionInDays) < 90 | project title=name, detail=strcat('Retention ', tostring(properties.retentionInDays), ' days (below 90)'), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each workspace, raise the default data retention to at least 90 days. Portal: Azure portal > Log Analytics workspaces > workspace > Settings > Usage and estimated costs > Data Retention. CLI: az monitor log-analytics workspace update -g <rg> --workspace-name <ws> --retention-time 90
checks.impact: Sub-90-day log retention deletes the evidence trail before most incidents are even detected.
checks.best_practice: Keep at least 90 days of log retention so the evidence trail outlives the typical gap between a breach and its discovery; extend further, using cheaper archive tiers, where a compliance regime or your own investigation needs demand it.
checks.blurb: Log Analytics workspaces whose interactive retention is set below 90 days.

checks.label: NSG rules exposing UDP to the internet
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | mv-expand rule=properties.securityRules | where tostring(rule.properties.direction) =~ 'Inbound' and tostring(rule.properties.access) =~ 'Allow' and tostring(rule.properties.protocol) in~ ('UDP','*') and tostring(rule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix) in ('*','0.0.0.0/0','Internet') | project title=name, detail=strcat('Rule ', tostring(rule.name), ' allows inbound UDP from ', tostring(rule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id=strcat(tostring(id), '/securityRules/', tostring(rule.name))
checks.fix: On each flagged rule, change Source from Any/Internet to the specific ranges that need the UDP service, and set Protocol to TCP where UDP is not required. Portal: Azure portal > Network security groups > [NSG] > Inbound security rules. CLI: az network nsg rule update -g <rg> --nsg-name <nsg> -n <rule> --source-address-prefixes <cidr>.
checks.impact: UDP services open to the internet are reachable for amplification abuse and direct exploitation from anywhere.
checks.best_practice: Scope inbound UDP rules to the specific source ranges that need them rather than the whole internet, so exposed UDP services cannot be abused for amplification or exploited from anywhere.
checks.blurb: NSG inbound Allow rules that permit UDP (or any protocol) from the internet or any source.

checks.label: Private DNS zones linked to spoke VNets instead of the hub
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | where array_length(properties.virtualNetworkPeerings) == 1 | mv-expand peering=properties.virtualNetworkPeerings | project spokeId=tolower(tostring(id)), spokeName=name, hubId=tolower(tostring(peering.properties.remoteVirtualNetwork.id)) | join kind=inner (resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | where array_length(properties.virtualNetworkPeerings) > 1 | project hubId=tolower(tostring(id)), hubName=name) on hubId | join kind=inner (resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privatednszones/virtualnetworklinks' | project linkId=id, linkRg=resourceGroup, linkSub=subscriptionId, zone=extract('/privatednszones/([^/]+)/', 1, tolower(tostring(id))), zoneParent=substring(tolower(tostring(id)), 0, indexof(tolower(tostring(id)), '/virtualnetworklinks')), spokeId=tolower(tostring(properties.virtualNetwork.id))) on spokeId | join kind=leftouter (resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privatednszones/virtualnetworklinks' | project zoneParent=substring(tolower(tostring(id)), 0, indexof(tolower(tostring(id)), '/virtualnetworklinks')), hubId=tolower(tostring(properties.virtualNetwork.id)), hubLinked=1) on zoneParent, hubId | where isnull(hubLinked) | project title=zone, detail=strcat('Linked directly to spoke VNet ', spokeName, ' (peered to hub ', hubName, ')'), rtype='microsoft.network/privateDnsZones/virtualNetworkLinks', rg=linkRg, sub=linkSub, id=linkId
checks.fix: Link each zone to the hub VNet, set the spokes' custom DNS to the hub resolver or forwarders, then remove the spoke link. Portal: Azure portal > Private DNS zones > [zone] > DNS Management > Virtual Network Links. CLI: az network private-dns link vnet delete -g <rg> -z <zone> -n <link>.
checks.impact: DNS resolution is scattered across the spokes instead of the hub, so name resolution depends on which spoke happens to hold a link; zones get duplicated, records drift apart, and a workload moved to another spoke silently stops resolving its private endpoints.
checks.best_practice: In a hub-and-spoke topology the hub is the centre of DNS resolution: private DNS zones are hosted centrally and linked to the hub VNet only, and spokes resolve through the hub (Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint, or DNS forwarders, set as the spokes' custom DNS). Linking zones to individual spokes spreads authority for private-endpoint names across the app teams' own networks, where it drifts and duplicates. Spoke links are only expected where a spoke is deliberately its own DNS island. A zone that carries BOTH a hub link and a spoke link is accepted (the hub path is already covered; the extra spoke link is a leftover, not a gap) and is excluded from this finding.
checks.blurb: Private DNS zone virtual-network links that point at a spoke VNet (a VNet with a single peering to a hub) rather than at the hub itself, and are NOT also linked to that hub.

checks.label: Subscriptions missing activity-log alerts for critical operations
checks.kql: resourcecontainers | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions' | project subscriptionId, subName=tostring(name) | extend required=dynamic(['microsoft.authorization/policyassignments/write','microsoft.authorization/policyassignments/delete','microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups/write','microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups/delete','microsoft.security/securitysolutions/write','microsoft.security/securitysolutions/delete','microsoft.sql/servers/firewallrules/write','microsoft.network/publicipaddresses/write','microsoft.network/publicipaddresses/delete']) | mv-expand op=required to typeof(string) | join kind=leftouter (resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | mv-expand cond=properties.condition.allOf | where tolower(tostring(cond.field)) == 'operationname' | project subscriptionId, op=tolower(tostring(cond.equals)), present=1) on subscriptionId, op | extend gap=iff(isnull(present), 1, 0) | summarize nops=count(), gaps=sum(gap) by subscriptionId, subName | where gaps > 0 | project title=coalesce(subName, subscriptionId), detail=strcat(gaps, ' of ', nops, ' critical operations have no activity-log alert'), sub=subscriptionId
checks.fix: In each subscription, create activity-log alert rules for the missing critical operations (policy, NSG, security solution, SQL firewall, public IP writes/deletes), routed to a monitored action group. Portal: Azure portal > Monitor > Alerts > Create > Alert rule, condition signal Activity log.
checks.impact: These alerts are the only near-real-time signal that someone weakened the security configuration; without them changes go unnoticed.
checks.best_practice: Configure activity-log alerts on the control-plane operations that weaken security posture, routed to an action group your team monitors, so a change to a firewall, NSG, policy, or public IP raises a near-real-time signal instead of passing unnoticed.
checks.blurb: Subscriptions missing activity-log alerts for one or more security-critical control-plane operations (policy, NSG, security solution, SQL firewall, and public IP changes).

checks.label: AKS clusters with local (non-Entra) accounts enabled
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' | where tostring(properties.disableLocalAccounts) != 'true' | project title=name, detail='Local cluster admin accounts are enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Disable local accounts on each Entra-enabled cluster, then rotate cluster certificates to revoke previously issued static credentials. Portal: no portal toggle, CLI only. CLI: az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --disable-local-accounts.
checks.impact: A local cluster certificate bypasses Entra sign-in entirely, so it inherits none of your MFA or Conditional Access, and its use leaves no trace in the tenant sign-in logs.
checks.best_practice: Disable local accounts and authenticate to the cluster with Entra ID, so cluster access is governed by the same identity controls, MFA and audit trail as everything else in the tenant.
checks.blurb: AKS clusters where the built-in local admin accounts (clusterAdmin/clusterUser certificates) have not been disabled.

checks.label: Container registries reachable from any network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerregistry/registries' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | project title=name, detail='Public network access is enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each registry, set Public network access to Disabled and reach it via a private endpoint (Premium SKU); on Basic/Standard use an IP allow-list instead. Portal: Azure portal > Container registry > Settings > Networking > Public access. CLI: az acr update -n <registry> --public-network-enabled false.
checks.impact: A registry open to the internet lets anyone who obtains a credential pull your images, and images routinely embed configuration, dependencies and occasionally secrets.
checks.best_practice: Reach registries over a private endpoint and disable public network access. Private access requires the Premium SKU, so on Basic and Standard registries the honest alternative is a tight IP allow-list.
checks.blurb: Azure Container Registries whose public network access is enabled rather than restricted to a private endpoint.

checks.label: Application Gateways on a WAF SKU with no WAF protection
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/applicationgateways' | where tostring(properties.sku.tier) contains 'WAF' | where isnull(properties.firewallPolicy) | where tostring(properties.webApplicationFirewallConfiguration.enabled) != 'true' | project title=name, detail='WAF SKU but no firewall policy and WAF config disabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Attach a WAF policy to each flagged gateway, creating one and adding the gateway on the policy's Association tab if none exists. Portal: Azure portal > Create a resource > Web Application Firewall > Create > Association > Add association > Application Gateway.
checks.impact: You are paying the WAF SKU premium while every request reaches the application unfiltered, so the protection the architecture diagram claims does not exist.
checks.best_practice: A gateway on a WAF SKU should always have a WAF policy attached. If it does not, the SKU is being paid for and not used.
checks.blurb: Application Gateways provisioned on a WAF SKU that have neither a firewall policy attached nor the inline WAF configuration enabled.

checks.label: WAF policies running in Detection mode
checks.kql: resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.network/applicationgatewaywebapplicationfirewallpolicies','microsoft.network/frontdoorwebapplicationfirewallpolicies') | where tostring(properties.policySettings.mode) !~ 'Prevention' | project title=name, detail=strcat('Policy mode is ', iff(isempty(tostring(properties.policySettings.mode)), '(unset)', tostring(properties.policySettings.mode))), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each WAF policy, review the logged matches, clear false positives with exclusions, then set Policy mode to Prevention. Portal: Azure portal > Web Application Firewall policies > [policy] > Overview > Switch to prevention mode.
checks.impact: In Detection mode the WAF writes the attack to a log and forwards it to the application anyway, so an attack that is fully understood still succeeds.
checks.best_practice: Detection mode is a tuning phase, not a destination. Run it long enough to clear the false positives, then switch to Prevention, otherwise the WAF only records the breach.
checks.blurb: Application Gateway and Front Door WAF policies whose mode is Detection (log only) rather than Prevention (block).

checks.label: Virtual machines without Trusted Launch
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' | where tostring(properties.securityProfile.securityType) !~ 'TrustedLaunch' and tostring(properties.securityProfile.securityType) !~ 'ConfidentialVM' | project title=name, detail=strcat('securityType=', iff(isempty(tostring(properties.securityProfile.securityType)), '(not set)', tostring(properties.securityProfile.securityType))), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Stop each Gen2 VM and change Security type to Trusted launch with Secure Boot and vTPM enabled; convert Gen1 VMs to Gen2 first. Portal: Azure portal > Virtual machines > VM (stopped) > Overview > Security type > Configuration. CLI: az vm update -g <rg> -n <vm> --security-type TrustedLaunch --enable-secure-boot true --enable-vtpm true.
checks.impact: Without Secure Boot and a vTPM there is nothing to stop a rootkit or a tampered boot loader from loading before the operating system, and nothing to attest that the machine booted clean.
checks.best_practice: Enable Trusted Launch on every Gen2 VM: it costs nothing and gives you Secure Boot, a vTPM and boot integrity monitoring. Gen1 machines need converting to Gen2 first, which is why this is a project rather than a switch.
checks.blurb: Virtual machines not deployed with Trusted Launch (Secure Boot + vTPM) or as a Confidential VM. Generation 1 VMs cannot use it without conversion.

checks.label: Custom roles granting all actions (*)
checks.kql: authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roledefinitions' | where tostring(properties.type) =~ 'CustomRole' | mv-expand perm=properties.permissions | mv-expand action=perm.actions | where tostring(action) == '*' | project title=tostring(properties.roleName), detail='Custom role grants * (every action)', sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: Edit each custom role to replace the * action with the explicit actions it needs, or reassign a built-in role. Portal: Azure portal > Subscriptions > Access control (IAM) > Roles > filter Type = CustomRole > ... > Edit > Permissions.
checks.impact: A custom role granting * is Owner wearing a harmless name, so it survives the review that would have caught an Owner assignment.
checks.best_practice: Custom roles should enumerate the actions they need. A wildcard defeats the reason for creating a custom role, and it hides an Owner-equivalent grant from anyone auditing Owner assignments.
checks.blurb: Custom RBAC role definitions whose permissions include the wildcard action *, making them equivalent to Owner.

checks.label: SQL servers allowing TLS below 1.2
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers' | where tostring(properties.minimalTlsVersion) in ('1.0','1.1','None') | project title=name, detail=strcat('minimalTlsVersion=', tostring(properties.minimalTlsVersion)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each SQL logical server, set Minimum TLS Version to 1.2. Portal: Azure portal > SQL server > Security > Networking > Connectivity tab. CLI: az sql server update -n <server> -g <rg> --set minimalTlsVersion=1.2.
checks.impact: The older TLS versions have known weaknesses, so a database connection negotiated down to them can be read in transit.
checks.best_practice: Require TLS 1.2 as the minimum. The older versions have known, exploited weaknesses and every supported client driver already speaks 1.2.
checks.blurb: Azure SQL logical servers whose minimum TLS version is 1.0, 1.1 or unset (None).

checks.label: MySQL / PostgreSQL servers with SSL enforcement disabled
checks.kql: resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.dbformysql/servers','microsoft.dbforpostgresql/servers') | where tostring(properties.sslEnforcement) =~ 'Disabled' | project title=name, detail='SSL enforcement is disabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each legacy MySQL or PostgreSQL single server, set sslEnforcement to Enabled, and plan migration off the retired Single Server tier. Portal: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Recommendations (Enforce SSL connection should be enabled). CLI: Update-AzMySqlServer -ResourceGroupName <rg> -Name <server> -SslEnforcement Enabled.
checks.impact: With enforcement off the server accepts plaintext connections, so credentials and query results cross the network in the clear and anyone on the path can read them.
checks.best_practice: Require SSL/TLS on every database connection. On Flexible Server the equivalent is the require_secure_transport parameter, which has to be checked on the server itself.
checks.blurb: Single-server MySQL and PostgreSQL instances that accept unencrypted connections. Flexible Server exposes this as a server parameter, which Resource Graph cannot see.

checks.label: Cosmos DB accounts reachable from any network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | project title=name, detail='Public network access is enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each Cosmos DB account, disable public network access and use a private endpoint, or set Allow access from to Selected networks with an IP allow-list. Portal: Azure portal > Cosmos DB account > Networking. CLI: az cosmosdb update -g <rg> -n <account> --public-network-access Disabled.
checks.impact: The account's data endpoint answers from anywhere on the internet, so a leaked key or connection string is immediately usable by whoever holds it.
checks.best_practice: Disable public network access and use a private endpoint. Where that is impractical, an IP firewall plus VNet service endpoints is the minimum, since a Cosmos key alone is otherwise enough to read the data from anywhere.
checks.blurb: Cosmos DB accounts whose public network access is enabled rather than restricted to a private endpoint or an allow-list.

checks.label: Redis caches allowing TLS below 1.2
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.cache/redis' | where tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion) in ('1.0','1.1') | project title=name, detail=strcat('minimumTlsVersion=', tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each cache, set Minimum TLS version to 1.2. Portal: Azure portal > Azure Cache for Redis > Settings > Advanced settings > Minimum TLS version. CLI: Set-AzRedisCache -Name <cache> -MinimumTlsVersion '1.2'.
checks.impact: A cache reachable over TLS 1.0 lets an attacker on the network path downgrade the connection and read whatever the application keeps in it, which is usually session and identity data.
checks.best_practice: Require TLS 1.2 as the minimum on the cache, and keep the non-SSL port closed. The two settings are independent, and closing one without the other leaves the connection downgradeable.
checks.blurb: Redis caches whose minimum TLS version is 1.0 or 1.1. Separate from the non-SSL port check, which is about the port, not the protocol version.

checks.label: Service Bus / Event Hub namespaces allowing TLS below 1.2
checks.kql: resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.servicebus/namespaces','microsoft.eventhub/namespaces') | where tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion) in ('1.0','1.1') | project title=name, detail=strcat('minimumTlsVersion=', tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion)), rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each namespace, set the minimum TLS version to 1.2. Portal: Azure portal > Service Bus or Event Hubs namespace > Settings > Configuration > Minimum TLS version.
checks.impact: Messages in transit carry the business event itself, so a downgraded connection exposes the payload and the SAS token that fetched it.
checks.best_practice: Require TLS 1.2 as the minimum on messaging namespaces. Clients that cannot negotiate it are old enough that the connection string they carry is likely also overdue for rotation.
checks.blurb: Service Bus and Event Hub namespaces whose minimum TLS version is 1.0 or 1.1.

checks.label: App Services reachable from any network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'Enabled' | project title=name, detail='Public network access is explicitly enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each App Service, set Public network access to Disabled and reach it via a private endpoint, or front it with Front Door or Application Gateway plus access restrictions. Portal: Azure portal > App Services > app > Settings > Networking > Inbound traffic configuration > Public network access.
checks.impact: An app answering directly on the internet is reachable by every scanner on it, and any WAF you have bought sits beside the traffic rather than in front of it.
checks.best_practice: Put a private endpoint in front of internal apps and route public ones through Front Door or Application Gateway, so the origin itself never answers the internet directly.
checks.blurb: App Services whose publicNetworkAccess is explicitly Enabled. Sites that leave the property unset are not flagged, since that is the default for most plans.

checks.label: Automation accounts reachable from any network
checks.kql: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.automation/automationaccounts' | where tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess) =~ 'true' | project title=name, detail='Public network access is enabled', rtype=type, rg=resourceGroup, sub=subscriptionId, id
checks.fix: On each Automation account, set Public Network Access to No and reach the account through a private endpoint (with hybrid workers for runbooks). Portal: Azure portal > Automation accounts > account > Account Settings > Network Isolation > Public Network Access: No.
checks.impact: An Automation account holds credentials and runbooks that act on your subscription, so reaching it from the internet is reaching the thing that can change everything else.
checks.best_practice: Disable public network access on Automation accounts and reach them over a private endpoint, because a runbook's whole purpose is privileged action on the subscription.
checks.blurb: Automation accounts whose public network access is enabled rather than restricted to a private endpoint.

checks.label: Management group hierarchy exists
checks.fix: Create a management-group hierarchy (e.g. Platform, Landing Zones, Sandbox) and move subscriptions under it so policy and access are inherited. Portal: Azure portal > All services > Management + governance > Management Groups > + Add management group. CLI: New-AzManagementGroup -GroupName <name>.
checks.impact: Without a management-group structure you must repeat every security and cost rule per subscription, and they inevitably drift apart.
checks.best_practice: More than just the Tenant Root group: a small hierarchy that separates shared platform subscriptions from your workload landing zones, with a sandbox for experiments. Two or three tiers is usually enough. Once it exists, security, cost, and access rules are set once at the group level and inherited by every subscription beneath, instead of being copied and left to drift.
checks.blurb: All subscriptions sit directly under the Tenant Root group (no landing-zone hierarchy).

checks.label: Azure Policy non-compliant resources
checks.fix: Create remediation tasks on the non-compliant deployIfNotExists/modify assignments and fix the rest manually; assign baseline initiatives at management-group scope so new resources auto-remediate. Portal: Azure portal > Policy > Remediation > select policy > Remediate.
checks.impact: Resources failing your own policies mean the guardrails exist but nothing behind them is being enforced or fixed.
checks.best_practice: Aim for zero non-compliant resources, but the target that keeps it there is enforcement rather than clean-up: assign baseline policy initiatives at the management-group level and let deployIfNotExists or modify effects auto-remediate, so new resources are brought into line as they are created instead of being caught after the fact.
checks.blurb: Resources failing assigned Azure Policy, per subscription.

checks.label: Subscriptions without a budget
checks.fix: Create a Cost Management budget on each subscription, amount set to its normal run rate, with staged alert thresholds (e.g. 50/75/90%) and email recipients. Portal: Azure portal > Cost Management + Billing > Subscriptions > select subscription > Budgets > Add.
checks.impact: Without a budget or alert, your first sign of a runaway resource is the invoice.
checks.best_practice: One Cost Management budget per subscription, each with staged alert thresholds (for example 50, 75, and 90 percent of the expected spend) so someone is warned while there is still time to act, rather than after the month has closed. Set the amount to the subscription's normal run rate so an alert genuinely signals something unusual.
checks.blurb: Subscriptions with no Cost Management budget / alert configured.

checks.label: Subscriptions without activity-log diagnostics
checks.fix: On each subscription, add a diagnostic setting that exports the Activity Log to a central Log Analytics workspace (add storage or event hub if longer retention or streaming is needed). Portal: Azure portal > Monitor > Activity log > Export Activity Logs > Add diagnostic setting.
checks.impact: If the activity log is not kept anywhere, you cannot reconstruct who changed what after an incident.
checks.best_practice: Every subscription should route its activity log to a central Log Analytics workspace, with a storage account or event hub added where longer retention or downstream streaming is needed. Keep at least a year, and preferably longer, because the workspace's own default retention is short and incidents are often investigated months after the change that caused them.
checks.blurb: Subscriptions not exporting the activity log to a Log Analytics workspace, storage account, or event hub.

checks.label: Classic (co-)administrators still present
checks.fix: Classic admin roles are fully retired; remaining Co/Service Administrators were auto-converted to subscription-scope Owner. Remove or downgrade those converted Owner assignments to scoped RBAC roles. Portal: Azure portal > Subscriptions > Access control (IAM) > Role assignments > select > Remove.
checks.impact: Classic administrators bypass your modern role controls and often outlive the people you created them for.
checks.best_practice: None. The classic administrator model predates Azure RBAC and grants unscoped, subscription-wide control that cannot be limited to a resource group or reviewed like a normal role assignment. Microsoft has retired it, so any account still holding a classic role should be moved to a scoped RBAC role and the classic entry removed.

checks.label: Reserved VM instance coverage
checks.fix: Where units are short, buy a 1- or 3-year reservation sized to the steady-state count, at Shared scope for cross-subscription coverage (Azure portal > All services > Reservations > Add > Virtual machine). Where units are idle, fix the reason before assuming you over-bought: switch the reservation to Shared scope if matching VMs run in another subscription, turn instance size flexibility On so it follows resizes within the size group, or exchange it for the size and region you actually run (Reservations > select > Configuration / Exchange). Restart or right-size deallocated machines, or exchange the surplus down. Turn auto-renew on for anything expiring that you still need.
checks.impact: Both halves of the reservation bill leak money: units you bought and nobody is using, and machines paying on-demand rates beside them.
checks.best_practice: Reserved units should track the steady-state running footprint of each region and VM size-flexibility group, measured in flexibility ratio units rather than machine counts: eight Standard_D2s_v5 and four Standard_D4s_v5 consume exactly the same reservation. Buy at shared scope so the discount floats across subscriptions, leave instance size flexibility on so it follows resizes, and size the quantity to the machines that genuinely run continuously. A reservation is a fixed hourly commitment, so an idle unit costs the same as a used one: deallocating a machine does not save money while its reservation keeps billing, and once the running footprint outgrows the reservation the excess quietly reverts to on-demand rates.
checks.blurb: Reserved units against running units per region and VM size-flexibility group: reservations sitting idle, machines running past the reservation on pay-as-you-go, wrong applied scope, flexibility switched off, expiries, and purchase candidates.
